article_title: Expository Reading and Writing Course (ERWC)
citation: Expository Reading and Writing Course (ERWC). (2015). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Expository+Reading+and+Writing+Course
title: ERWC instructional focus on discussion, critical thinking, oral language, genre writing, and rhetorical analysis
description: The ERWC's design centers English instruction on a set of interrelated practices: "discussions of text meaning, developing critical thinking skills, encouraging group discussions, developing oral language skills, developing writing skills in multiple genres, and analyzing the rhetorical features of texts and applying them in student writing." These foci operate across the whole twelfth-grade English course.
requirements: Teachers deliver the ERWC curriculum materials with professional learning and coaching support.
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
critical thinking
academic writing
oral language
rhetorical analysis
examples: The course replaces ordinary twelfth-grade English classes and applies these foci throughout the year.

article_title: Evaluation of the Expository Reading and Writing Course: Findings from the Investing in Innovation Development Grant
citation: Anthony B. Fong, Neal D. Finkelstein, Laura M. Jaeger, Rebeca Diaz, Marie E. Broek. (2015). Evaluation of the Expository Reading and Writing Course: Findings from the Investing in Innovation Development Grant. WestEd. http://www.WestEd.org
title: ERWC logic model: curriculum, professional learning, and materials as inputs leading to rhetorical classroom practices and improved college readiness
description: The ERWC theory holds that three inputs — curriculum, professional learning, and curriculum materials — produce classroom practices such as "extended discussion of text meaning and interpretation" to develop critical-thinking skills, interactive discussion to build oral language, and extended writing for varied tasks, purposes, and audiences. These practices are expected to yield improved outcomes measured by the EPT. The course rests on seven principles, including "A rhetorical approach that fosters critical thinking and engagement through a relentless focus on the text" and integration of interactive reading and writing processes.
requirements: Teachers must be certified through initial 20 hours of professional learning to teach the course
constraints: Designed for grade-12 students preparing for college-level English; targets expository, analytical, and argumentative reading and writing
target_learners: grade-12 high school students preparing for college-level English
target_learning_goals: critical reading and writing skills
rhetorical analysis of expository texts
college English readiness reducing remediation
examples: The course includes 12 modules organized by three domains — Reading Rhetorically, Connecting Reading to Writing, and Writing Rhetorically — with teachers expected to teach 8 to 10 modules

title: ERWC Assignment Template: scaffolded module structure with six strands across three domains
description: The ERWC curriculum's 12 modules all follow the Assignment Template, "which presents a scaffolded process to help students read, comprehend, and respond to nonfiction and literary texts." Each module spans three domains — Reading Rhetorically (Prereading, Reading, Postreading strands), Connecting Reading to Writing (Discovering What You Think), and Writing Rhetorically (Entering the Conversation, Revising and Editing). Strands contain elements with activities, such as Surveying the Text and Making Predictions and Asking Questions. The template also embeds formative assessment recommendations and rhetorical grammar activities using curriculum readings and students' own writings.
requirements: Teachers are expected to teach 8 to 10 of the 12 modules over the school year, including one full-length book per semester
constraints: In some modules a given element may contain multiple activities, and in others an element may include no activities for the teacher to complete
target_learning_goals: reading and comprehending nonfiction and literary texts
rhetorical reading and writing
academic writing conventions
examples: The Prereading strand includes elements such as Getting Ready to Read, Exploring Key Concepts, Surveying the Text, Making Predictions and Asking Questions, and Understanding Key Vocabulary

article_title: Fairness Theatre: Evaluating Post-Hoc Fairness Interventions in Vendor-Controlled Early Warning Systems
citation: McConvey, K., Zhai, A., Li, R., & Guha, S. (2026). Fairness Theatre: Evaluating Post-Hoc Fairness Interventions in Vendor-Controlled Early Warning Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38552
title: Error-type profiling: translating fairness metrics into the errors advisors and students encounter
description: Error-type profiling is the analytic lens the article introduces to judge fairness interventions by how they redistribute false positives and false negatives across groups, rather than only by whether fairness metrics converge. The article introduces it as "a lens that translates fairness metrics into the terms advisors actually encounter: which students appear on caseloads and which are never seen." With predicted-successful as the positive class, a false negative is a successful student predicted at-risk who occupies a scarce advising slot and risks stigmatization, while a false positive is a struggling student predicted successful who never appears on any advisor's caseload.
requirements: Access to group-level error rates (TPR, FPR, positive classification rate) on model outputs, and a defined workflow consequence for each error type
constraints: The article evaluates error redistribution under a single-axis demographic framework that cannot capture compounding disadvantages for intersectional students
target_learners: College students subject to early warning risk flagging, and the advisors acting on flagged caseloads
target_learning_goals: Fair distribution of false positives and false negatives in predictive student-support triage
examples: The article evaluated each of the six interventions by how it redistributes errors across types and groups, asking whether fairness gains reflect genuine improvement or merely shift which students bear which errors

article_title: How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops -- A Taxonomy
citation: Dimitri Eckert and Christian Kautz. (2026). How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops – A Taxonomy. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26966v1
title: Distinctions among error, difficulty, and misconception, with misconceptions as potentially fragile knowledge
description: The article defines a terminology framework for classifying student problems: an error is a concrete incidence of a mistake, a difficulty is the underlying misunderstanding or erroneous cognitive behavior that causes errors, and a misconception is a difficulty grounded in an incorrect mental model. The authors define a misconception as "a specific kind of difficulty that is based in a concrete mental model about a specific programming concept that does not align with reality". They also argue misconceptions need not be stable, challenging prior definitions.
requirements: The terms must be used distinctly to avoid confusion, since they are sometimes used interchangeably in the literature
constraints: The authors challenge the definition that misconceptions are necessarily stable and systematically repeated, noting novice programming misconceptions can be fragile knowledge
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of programming constructs
examples: The framework treats misconceptions as non-binary, allowing students to hold semi-correct or multiple notions of a concept at the same time

article_title: Effects of extensive reading on reading attitudes in a foreign language
citation: Junko Yamashita. (2013). Effects of extensive reading on reading attitudes in a foreign language. Reading in a Foreign Language, 25(2). http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl
title: 15-week university extensive reading course with free choice of graded readers and book reports
description: A 15-week compulsory EFL course at a Japanese university met weekly for 90 minutes; "During class, students were able to access approximately 500 graded English readers (a series of Oxford, Cambridge, Heinemann, and Penguin), and were encouraged to choose whichever books they wanted to read." The class split between administration/activities and free voluntary silent reading; students submitted a B5-size book report per book as the credit requirement and were graded on participation and amount read. Students read 649 pages (SD = 201), about 13 readers or 120,634 words, on average.
requirements: A library of graded readers at varied levels must be accessible, and book reports were required for credit
constraints: The author states results are an outcome of this study's context and generalizability to other educational and socio-cultural circumstances may be limited
target_learners: Second-year Japanese university undergraduates learning EFL
target_learning_goals: Improved L2 reading attitudes (comfort, anxiety, intellectual value) through sustained extensive reading
examples: All students chose to write their book reports in Japanese, and five students additionally read their own paperbacks outside the graded-reader stock

article_title: Effects of extensive reading on reading attitudes in a foreign language
citation: Junko Yamashita. (2013). Effects of extensive reading on reading attitudes in a foreign language. Reading in a Foreign Language, 25(2). http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl
title: Best-practice circumstances for implementing extensive reading in reading classes
description: The article enumerates the circumstances under which classes that incorporate ER best operate, following Day and Bamford (2002): "a variety of reading materials are available on a wide range of topics at different levels of linguistic difficulty; students choose what they want to read, read unassisted, and view reading as its own reward." It adds that students often read faster because they select materials of interest at an appropriate difficulty level, and teachers act as model readers who guide rather than explicitly teach. The study's own course instantiated these circumstances.
requirements: A variety of reading materials across topics and difficulty levels must be available; students must be able to choose their own books and read unassisted
constraints: The article notes there are different ways of implementing ER (e.g., exclusively outside class or using only a small portion of class time), so the pattern is one implementation among several
target_learners: L2/EFL learners in classroom reading programs
target_learning_goals: Developing good reading habits, liking for reading, and L2 reading attitude
examples: In the study's course, the latter half of each 90-minute class was devoted to free, voluntary silent reading at students' own pace, with the teacher answering questions individually and advising

article_title: Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise
citation: M. Gartmeier, J. Bauer, H. Gruber, H. Heid. (2008). Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise. Vocations and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12186-008-9006-1
title: Error-related learning as experiential learning producing negative knowledge through analysis, reflection, regret and correction
description: The article conceptualizes learning from errors at work as a special form of experiential learning in which errors challenge individual mental models and provide starting points for modification — through differentiation, replacement of parts, or indexing weak areas. Analysis and reflection are crucial mediating activities, and Oser and Spychiger propose that "regret and correction are required for building negative knowledge from an error". Bauer and Mulder's framework involves cause analysis, developing new avoidance strategies, and experimentation with implementation.
requirements: Reflection and analysis of the error episode; regret and correction per Oser and Spychiger
constraints: What constitutes an error involves norm-based judgments that may differ substantially between workplaces and individuals
target_learning_goals: learning from errors
building negative knowledge
professional development
examples: Flight simulator training lets pilots learn from almost authentic critical experience without fatal consequences, building procedural negative knowledge

article_title: Errors During Exploration and Consolidation—The Effectiveness of Productive Failure as Sequentially Guided Discovery Learning
citation: Julie McNamara and Meghan M. Shaughnessy. (2011). Student errors: What can they tell us about what students DO understand? Math Solutions. https://www.mathsolutions.com
title: Errors as partial understandings: incorrect responses as normal parts of developing understanding
description: The article advances the view, drawing on Saxe et al. (2010) and Wells & Coffey (2005), that student errors are often "partial understandings" or "correct answers to slightly different questions" rather than carelessness or global misunderstanding. Exposing and discussing these responses is presented as productive for deepening and refining students' thinking. Teachers are urged to acknowledge what students do know and build on it.
requirements: Teachers must interpret the specific reasoning behind a response rather than dismissing it as careless or globally wrong
constraints: The article frames this as a practitioner perspective drawing on cited research rather than reporting new empirical data of its own
target_learners: elementary and middle school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: fraction understanding
rational number concepts
examples: A student answering 1/3 for a shaded region showing one of four parts demonstrates correct conventional fraction notation but incomplete part-whole reasoning

article_title: The influence of retrieval on retention
citation: Carrier, M., & Pashler, H. (1992). The influence of retrieval on retention. Memory & Cognition, 20(6), 633-642. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03204076
title: Error-correction learning models account for the retrieval advantage; Hebbian-type models do not
description: The article proposes that network models with error-correction learning (e.g., McClelland & Rumelhart, 1986) naturally explain why retrieval beats study: an attempted retrieval generates an estimate of the response, and connections are modified to reduce the error between that estimate and the canonical representation. Presenting the response itself may "contaminate" the estimate, reducing learning in the pure ST condition, an account the authors compare to associative blocking in Pavlovian conditioning. By contrast, the authors argue it is "not clear why memory storage would be more effective when the subject was deprived of one of the patterns to be associated" under Hebbian and other distributed models.
requirements: Learners must generate a response estimate during the trial so that error correction against the canonical representation can occur
constraints: The authors state the present results and analyses do not provide sufficient information to distinguish between direct retrieval contributions to learning and the error-correction account, and that the concept of a retrieval route is inherently vague
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of paired associations
examples: The article maps the account onto the Rescorla/Wagner model of blocking, where conditioning to CS1 is reduced when the US is already expected from CS2
key_sources: Carrier, M., & Pashler, H. (1992). The influence of retrieval on retention. Memory & Cognition, 20(6), 633-642. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03202713

article_title: Delayed Learning Effects with Erroneous Examples: a Study of Learning Decimals with a Web-Based Tutor
citation: Bruce M. McLaren & Deanne M. Adams & Richard E. Mayer. (2015). Delayed Learning Effects with Erroneous Examples: a Study of Learning Decimals with a Web-Based Tutor. International Artificial Intelligence in Education Society 2015. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0064-x
title: Erroneous examples as a desirable difficulty that promotes generative processing and durable learning
description: The article proposes that prompting students to identify, explain, and fix errors in someone else's solution primes deeper cognitive processing than solving problems alone. Erroneous example study "involves elements of both example studyand problem solving" and may strengthen "don't do X" knowledge alongside procedural knowledge, developing multiple cognitive paths. Learning from erroneous examples "can be seen as similar to a desirable difficulty," explained via cognitive load theory's generative/germane processing, producing delayed but not immediate learning benefits.
requirements: Students must be prompted to actively identify, explain, and fix errors rather than passively view erroneous solutions
Correctness feedback is needed so students do not learn the incorrect way to solve problems
constraints: Evidence so far shows the benefit on delayed tests given a week later, not on immediate tests
Demonstrated for a single middle-school decimals topic with mostly single-step problems
target_learning_goals: decimal number concepts and procedures
overcoming common decimal misconceptions
examples: Students reviewed a fictional student's error, identified the misconception from options, fixed the solution, and explained the correct procedure, with correctness feedback at every step.
key_sources: Bruce M. McLaren & Deanne M. Adams & Richard E. Mayer. (2015). Delayed Learning Effects with Erroneous Examples: a Study of Learning Decimals with a Web-Based Tutor. International Artificial Intelligence in Education Society 2015. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0064-x

article_title: Delayed Learning Effects with Erroneous Examples: a Study of Learning Decimals with a Web-Based Tutor
citation: Bruce M. McLaren & Deanne M. Adams & Richard E. Mayer. (2015). Delayed Learning Effects with Erroneous Examples: a Study of Learning Decimals with a Web-Based Tutor. International Artificial Intelligence in Education Society 2015. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0064-x
title: Pair erroneous examples with correctness feedback so students cannot proceed with incorrect solutions
description: The article identifies feedback as a critical design condition for erroneous examples: "without feedback, students run the risk of learning the incorrect way to solve problems." In the study, students received correctness feedback on every step and "could not move forward until they had corrected errors and produced a correct solution strategy." This principle applies when implementing erroneous-example instruction with technology.
requirements: Correctness feedback on each student step
Gating so students correct errors and reach a correct solution before advancing
constraints: Demonstrated in a fast-paced, computer-based environment with menu-selected rather than generated self-explanations
target_learning_goals: correct decimal procedures and concepts
examples: In the study's tutor, answers turned green or red and a message window gave retry encouragement or success feedback at every selection step.

article_title: Effects of noise letters upon the identification of a target letter in a nonsearch task
citation: Eriksen, B. A., & Eriksen, C. W. (1974). Effects of noise letters upon the identification of a target letter in a nonsearch task. Perception & Psychophysics, 16(1), 143-149. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03203257
title: Limited-capacity visual attentional channel with response-selection locus of noise interference
description: The article proposes that visual attention has "a minimal channel size in terms of capacity for simultaneous processing with a capacity exceeding that required for identifying a single letter." Because this unutilized capacity cannot be shut off, letters within about 1 deg of the target are processed simultaneously with it and begin to evoke responses. A selection-and-inhibition process, keyed to the target's location, must then operate; it is slower at closer spacings and when noise indicates the opposite response. The data locate the noise effect at the response-selection stage rather than at input processing.
requirements: A target whose location is known and fixed, so that selection can be made by spatial position verification
constraints: The authors acknowledge a limited-energy parallel processing model could add an input-side decrement at the closest spacing, and that feature-detector submechanisms are not precluded
target_learners: adult laboratory subjects in visual information-processing experiments
target_learning_goals: understanding selective attention and visual information processing
examples: The nonsearch task eliminated visual search by presenting the target always Yz deg above the fixation point, isolating noise effects from search demands
key_sources: Eriksen, B. A., & Eriksen, C. W. (1974). Effects of noise letters upon the identification of a target letter in a nonsearch task. Perception & Psychophysics, 16(1), 143-149. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03203267

article_title: Effects of noise letters upon the identification of a target letter in a nonsearch task
citation: Eriksen, B. A., & Eriksen, C. W. (1974). Effects of noise letters upon the identification of a target letter in a nonsearch task. Perception & Psychophysics, 16(1), 143-149. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03203257
title: Eriksen and Eriksen nonsearch flanker paradigm (six-condition tachistoscopic letter task)
description: A tachistoscopic task in which the subject responds with a right or left leverpress to a single target letter (H or K vs S or C) that always appears at a fixed location above fixation during a 1-sec exposure. The target is flanked by three noise letters on each side under five noise conditions (identical, response-compatible, response-incompatible, heterogeneous-similar, heterogeneous-dissimilar) at three between-letter spacings (.06, Yz, and 1 deg of visual angle), plus mixed and blocked target-alone controls. It was designed to provide "an anchor or baseline condition" for noise effects when no visual search is required.
requirements: Subjects thoroughly instructed to respond only to the letter in the target location and ignore all other letters
constraints: Eliminating search removes the confounding of noise effects with assumptions about how display search is carried out, so findings are specific to the nonsearch case
target_learners: adult volunteers with normal or corrected-to-normal vision
target_learning_goals: studying the effects of noise stimuli on target identification independent of visual search
examples: Six experimental sessions of three 32-trial blocks plus one 12-trial single-letter block yielded 24 trials per subject per condition-by-spacing combination

article_title: Ethnic and Racial Identity During Adolescence and Into Young Adulthood: An Integrated Conceptualization
citation: Umaña-Taylor, A. J., Lee, R. M., Rivas-Drake, D., Syed, M., Seaton, E., Quintana, S. M., Cross, W. E. Jr., Schwartz, S. J., & Yip, T. (2014). Ethnic and Racial Identity During Adolescence and Into Young Adulthood: An Integrated Conceptualization. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12196
title: Ethnic-racial identity (ERI) as an integrated metaconstruct covering both ethnic background and racialized experiences
description: The Study Group proposes ERI as a single metaconstruct replacing the conventional split between racial identity and ethnic identity, arguing the distinction is largely nominal and the constructs overlap empirically. ERI is defined as "a multidimensional, psychological construct that reflects the beliefs and attitudes that individuals have about their ethnic–racial group memberships, as well as the processes by which these beliefs and attitudes develop over time." The term is proposed "to capture experiences that reflect both individuals’ ethnic background and their racialized experiences as a member of a particular group in the context of the United States." Components reflect content (beliefs, attitudes) and process (exploration, formation, maintenance), which are deeply intertwined.
requirements: Measures and studies must operationalize both content and process components of ERI rather than only self-categorization labels
constraints: Specificity to sociohistorical context is important; the authors note the proposal is grounded in the U.S. context, though similar processes may operate elsewhere
target_learners: ethnic and racial minority adolescents and young adults in the United States
target_learning_goals: understanding identity formation as a normative developmental process
understanding how beliefs and attitudes about one's ethnic-racial group develop over time
examples: The Study Group reviewed existing models (e.g., Phinney's ethnic identity model, Cross's nigrescence theory, Sellers et al.'s Multidimensional Model of Racial Identity) to build the integrated operationalization

article_title: Ethnic and Racial Identity During Adolescence and Into Young Adulthood: An Integrated Conceptualization
citation: Umaña-Taylor, A. J., Lee, R. M., Rivas-Drake, D., Syed, M., Seaton, E., Quintana, S. M., Cross, W. E. Jr., Schwartz, S. J., & Yip, T. (2014). title: Developmental timeline of ERI components: identification in childhood, exploration and internalization in adolescence, integration in adulthood
description: The article organizes ERI development across periods: childhood involves ethnic–racial labeling, knowledge, and constancy; adolescence adds exploration, centrality, affirmation, public regard, and salience as cognitive and perspective-taking capacities mature; young adulthood adds intersection with other identity domains and narrative coherence. The authors state that "the components of ERI that are relevant at specific developmental periods can be organized with attention to whether they primarily reflect the content of one’s ERI or the process of developing an ERI," and that ERI "is an interaction between maturation and context, and thus takes different forms and has different meanings across the life span."
requirements: Research must attend to which ERI components are developmentally salient in a given period rather than applying uniform measures across ages
constraints: Some components have been empirically examined only in relation to either ethnic or racial identity, not both
target_learners: young adults from ethnic-racial minority groups
target_learning_goals: understanding age-graded milestones in ethnic-racial identity formation
understanding how cognitive and social development enable identity exploration
examples: Table 1 organizes components by developmental period, distinguishing childhood ethnic–racial identification from adolescent ERI formation

article_title: Emotion Regulation Ability: Test Performance and Observer Reports in Predicting Relationship, Achievement and Well-Being Outcomes in Adolescents
citation: Ivcevic Zorana; Eggers Catherine. (2021). Emotion Regulation Ability: Test Performance and Observer Reports in Predicting Relationship, Achievement and Well-Being Outcomes in Adolescents. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8003666/
title: Emotion regulation ability as a maximal performance attribute distinct from typical performance self-reports
description: The article adopts a definition of emotion regulation as "a maximal performance attribute—an individual's ability to evaluate the effectiveness of different emotion regulation strategies". This contrasts with typical performance conceptualizations measured through self-report instruments asking about strategy frequency. Maximal performance ERA is assessed through ability tests presenting hypothetical emotion-laden scenarios where respondents judge how effective different actions would be toward achieving a specific regulation goal, scored against expert judgments. The article argues self-reports of emotion abilities are poor predictors because people are poor judges of their own emotion abilities.
requirements: Assessment requires ability tests presenting hypothetical emotion-laden situations with multiple response options
Scoring requires expert judgments guided by empirical research on effective emotion regulation strategies
constraints: Measures potential to evaluate strategies in hypothetical scenarios, not enacted regulation in daily situations
Self-report measures of emotion regulation ability are explicitly not employed due to poor predictive validity
target_learning_goals: evaluating effectiveness of emotion regulation strategies toward specific goals
examples: The MSCEIT-YV ERA subtest presents six emotion-filled hypothetical scenarios relevant to adolescents, each followed by three potential actions respondents judge for effectiveness

title: Three-mechanism theoretical rationale for extensive reading: implicit learning, comprehensible input, and motivation via choice
description: The article grounds extensive reading in three interrelated mechanisms. First, "extensive reading is expected to promote reading fluency by supporting implicit learning", via frequent exposure that strengthens lexical entries. Learner self-selection of reading material to support autonomous motivation

Students’ emotion regulation and school-related well-being:

                        perspectives.
citation: Beaumont, J., Putwain, D. W., Gallard, D., Malone, E., Marsh, H. W., & Pekrun, R. (2022, in press). Students' emotion regulation and school-related wellbeing: Longitudinal models juxtaposing between- and within-person perspectives. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://osf.io/W5CPE
title: Reciprocal reappraisal-wellbeing loop account grounded in Gross's process model, control-value theory, broaden-and-build theory, and the ERAS model
description: The article frames reappraisal-wellbeing reciprocity using Gross's process model of emotion regulation, which organizes strategies into "'antecedent-focused' strategies" implemented before the emotional response and "'response-focused' strategies" implemented after it, and Pekrun's control-value theory. It draws on Harley et al.'s (2019) emotion regulation in achievement situations (ERAS) model, in which control and value appraisals drive the cognitive-change stage, and on broaden-and-build theory, whereby wellbeing broadens cognition enabling positive reinterpretation. These accounts predict a reciprocal loop: reappraisal raises positive emotions and wellbeing, which in turn facilitate further positive reappraisal.
requirements: Requires that students can reframe control and value appraisals of academic situations (e.g., viewing an exam as an opportunity to demonstrate knowledge) before the emotional response develops
constraints: The article notes students have fewer regulation strategies available at school than outside it, limiting alternatives such as situation modification or distraction
target_learners: secondary and upper secondary students aged 11-19
target_learning_goals: school-related wellbeing
emotion regulation in academic situations
examples: The article illustrates ERAS with a student reminding themselves they have prior knowledge for a class discussion (a control appraisal increasing enjoyment) or that a boring lesson matters for an exam (a value appraisal reducing boredom)

article_title: Strategies for remediating the impact of math anxiety on high school math performance
citation: Rachel G. Pizzie and David J. M. Kraemer. (2023). Strategies for remediating the impact of math anxiety on high school math performance. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00188-5
title: Emotion Regulation intervention using cognitive reappraisal (emotional distancing and arousal reframing)
description: The Emotion Regulation (ER) intervention was a classroom adaptation of cognitive reappraisal, "a technique for reframing an anxious situation". It taught an emotional distancing strategy in which students "view the situation from a more objective perspective" (e.g., explaining the problem to a best friend), and a reframing technique treating physiological arousal as a challenge rather than an obstacle. Like the SS intervention, it was delivered in a 20–30 minute structured small-group discussion, followed by pre-test expressive writing about thoughts and feelings about the upcoming test and reappraisal strategies, plus reminders. The article reports this intervention was less efficacious for highly math-anxious students, whose anxiety-related grade declines persisted, though low-anxiety students in this group performed better.
requirements: Delivered as a structured small-group discussion with facilitator guidance and redirects for off-topic responses
Requires pre-test writing prompts about thoughts, feelings, and reappraisal strategies before exams
constraints: The article states cognitive reappraisal is a working-memory-intensive, effortful strategy that may be difficult to implement when cognitive resources are compromised by anxiety or when learning difficult new math skills; its benefits in this study accrued to low math-anxious students rather than highly anxious ones
target_learning_goals: Downregulating anxious responses to mathematics; reframing test-related emotional reactions to support math performance
examples: Students practiced reframing statements such as viewing the situation as a challenge rather than an obstacle, and wrote before tests about the thoughts and feelings they might experience and which reappraisal strategies they would use.

article_title: Quantifying two-dimensional and three-dimensional stereoscopic learning in anatomy using electroencephalography
citation: Anderson, S. J., Jamniczky, H. A., Krigolson, O. E., Coderre, S. P. & Hecker, K. G. (2019). Quantifying two-dimensional and three-dimensional stereoscopic learning in anatomy using electroencephalography. npj Science of Learning 4:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0050-4
title: ERP components (N250 and reward positivity) as quantitative neural markers of perceptual expertise and feedback-based learning
description: The article builds on a framework in which two event-related potential components track learning in reinforcement-based paradigms. The N250, measured over posterior scalp, "reflects the acquisition of long-term memory for perceptual categorization expertise at the subordinate (more detailed) level", while the reward positivity, measured at FCz, represents prediction error in response to positive feedback, and "the reduction in reward positivity amplitude re ﬂects an underlying learning process". The study applies these markers to anatomy learning to compare 2D, 3D, and interleaved stereoscopic conditions.
requirements: EEG recording during a reinforcement-based learning task with trial-and-error feedback, with enough error trials early in learning for difference-wave confirmation of the reward positivity
constraints: The authors note a possible threshold below which expertise cannot be distinguished by N250 amplitude, and that modules of 300 or fewer trials were too short to observe N250 increases with learning
target_learning_goals: identification and localization of neuroanatomical structures; perceptual expertise in object recognition
examples: Difference-wave analysis confirmed the reward positivity at peak latencies of 284 ms (2D), 296 ms (3D), and 284 ms (2D/3D), all p < 0.001

article_title: Protection of savings by reducing the salience of opposing errors
citation: Javidialsaadi, M., Albert, S. T., Al Mutairi, B. M. S., & Wang, J. (2025). Protection of savings by reducing the salience of opposing errors. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00352-z
title: Error-sensitivity account of savings with a proposed suppressive learning property opposing the memory-of-errors model
description: The article explains savings via a state-space model in which adaptation is "a recursive process controlled by two parameters: an error sensitivity (controls the amount of learning from error) and a retention factor". Savings after gradual learning reflects upregulated error sensitivity, which large oppositely signed washout errors reverse. The authors propose errors produce two effects: increased sensitivity to similar errors and suppression of sensitivity to opposite errors, challenging the locality property of the memory-of-errors model.
requirements: Requires fitting state-space models with both a retention parameter and an error-sensitivity parameter; the complete model was superior by AIC in 55 of 60 participants.
constraints: Implicit and explicit contributions were not measured, so the authors call their process-level hypothesis speculative and limited.
target_learners: healthy young adults performing visuomotor reaching tasks
target_learning_goals: sensorimotor adaptation and re-learning rate
examples: State-space model fits to exposure-2 learning curves showed error sensitivity elevated in the no-feedback washout group and not in the abrupt washout group.

citation: Nursultan Askarbekuly, Ivan Luković. (2024). Learning Outcomes, Assessment, and Evaluation in Educational Recommender Systems: A Systematic Review. https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09500
title: Three common approaches to implementing outcome-based assessment in ERS
description: The review outlines three approaches used within the reviewed ERS for outcome-based assessment: "outcomes and assessment were already in place as part of a formal course, or the assessment exercises automatically generated and graded, or their achievement was concluded from indirect observations". In the first, the system logs formal assessment results and optimizes recommendations accordingly, evaluating through experimental groups. In the second, a knowledge-based method models outcomes, assessment activities, and their relations within the system. In the third, traditional assessment is replaced with indirect measures indicative of learning, such as collaboration with other users.

examples: Three reviewed papers automated outcome-based assessment by linking parts of expected solutions to learning outcomes and updating the probability of achieving the outcome based on which parts of the program were written correctly

citation: Tuba Demircioglu, Sedat Ucar. (2015). Investigating the Effect of Argument-Driven Inquiry in Laboratory Instruction. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2015.1.2324
title: Five-level analytical framework for assessing argumentation quality (Toulmin-based)
description: The study scored student-written arguments using the framework of Erduran, Simon, and Osborne (2004), built on the Toulmin Model in which "data, claim, and warrants form the basis of an argument". constraints: Assumes arguments containing rebuttals are of higher quality; in this study no reports reached Level 5, so only the first four levels were used
target_learning_goals: argumentation quality in written scientific arguments
examples: Reports from the first, fourth, and last experiments were coded into Toulmin components and assigned levels; example reports at Levels 1 through 4 are printed in the article, and 48 data sets were double-coded with Cohen Kappa of .82.

requirements: Requires expert consensus on which procedural errors are serious enough to warrant a failure rating
constraints: Developed and tested only for lumbar puncture in a simulation-based examination; generalisability to other procedures or non-procedural skills may be limited
target_learning_goals: safe and competent performance of lumbar puncture
examples: Ratings of 18 video-recorded simulator LP performances using this tool were compared with ratings from a conventional 21-item checklist
key_sources: Ma Irene W Y, Pugh Debra, Mema Briseida, Brindle Mary E, Cooke Lara, Stromer Julie N. (2015). Use of an error-focused checklist to identify incompetence in lumbar puncture performances. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.12809
